A renovation budget needs payment dates and a contingency, not just a final price

Map deposit and progress payments, add an early extra bill, and compare the largest cash shortfall with the final project balance in four interactive charts.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore a renovation payment calendar and a cost overrun

Interactive planning lab

Hypothetical six-month construction period after the selected preparation months. Base price includes all known taxes and fees. The reference base-price schedule pays 10% at the deposit date, then 30% two, four and six months later; the alternative pays 50%, 25%, 15%, 10% on those same dates. These are invented comparison schedules, not recommended deposits or legal contract terms. The selected additional approved cost is paid one month after the deposit in both cases. Monthly saving arrives before that month’s bills; month zero has no saving receipt. Accessible project cash earns zero. The required extra is the largest negative project balance over the full calendar, with no automatic borrowing or cash injection. No financing, rebates, property-value gain, insurance claim, legal holdback or emergency fund is assumed. Preparation adds saving months; prices and the six-month build duration stay fixed.

The central idea

Two contracts can have the same total price and require different amounts of accessible cash. Fund the lowest point in the payment calendar as well as the total project cost.

01

Turn the project estimate into dated cash commitments

A renovation estimate answers how much a defined scope may cost. A household cash plan also asks when each amount becomes payable and which resources are accessible on that date. A final budget can look manageable while a deposit or material payment arrives before the next saving transfer.

The federal Office of Consumer Affairs home-renovation guide describes contract information including total cost, payment schedule, deposit, taxes and completion dates. These are useful inputs for a cash calendar. The charts do not interpret a contract or determine the payment and holdback rules in a particular province.

The example has a CAD 40,000 base price inclusive of all known taxes and fees. It then adds an independently selected 15% approved cost increase, or CAD 6,000. The resulting modeled cost is CAD 46,000. This extra-cost percentage is a stress assumption, not a prediction of typical renovation overruns or a statement that this reserve is sufficient for every project.

02

Keep the price fixed while changing the payment schedule

The reference schedule pays 10% of the base price at the deposit date and 30% at each of three milestones two, four and six months later. With immediate commencement, that means CAD 4,000 at month zero, followed by CAD 12,000 at months two, four and six.

The alternative pays 50%, 25%, 15% and 10% on those same dates: CAD 20,000, CAD 10,000, CAD 6,000 and CAD 4,000. Both schedules add to exactly the same CAD 40,000 base price. The purpose of the second schedule is to stress an earlier cash commitment; its large deposit is not presented as an appropriate contractual arrangement.

Both cases pay the CAD 6,000 extra bill one month after the deposit. Placing the same cost increase early in both calendars isolates the payment-schedule effect. In an actual project, the amount and due date of each approved change should be added to the calendar separately. An unapproved estimate increase is not automatically a payable household commitment merely because this model includes an assumed bill.

03

Find the largest funding gap, not only the last balance

The household starts with CAD 20,000 of accessible project cash and adds CAD 4,000 each month. Month zero has no saving receipt. In subsequent months, saving arrives before any bill due at that modeled date. This order must match reality before using the result; a bill due before pay arrives can require more cash.

Under the reference schedule, the immediate deposit leaves CAD 16,000. After the first monthly saving and the CAD 6,000 extra bill, cash is CAD 14,000. The month-two payment leaves CAD 6,000, and the final payment leaves a CAD 2,000 shortfall. The lowest point is therefore negative CAD 2,000.

Under the earlier-payment schedule, the deposit consumes the full starting cash balance. The extra bill brings month one to negative CAD 2,000. Month two reaches negative CAD 8,000, before the balance partly recovers. The final balance is again negative CAD 2,000. An endpoint-only calculation misses CAD 6,000 of the maximum interim funding need in this alternative.

04

Reconcile the total without assuming a loan appears

The waterfall adds CAD 20,000 of starting cash to six CAD 4,000 saving transfers, giving CAD 44,000 of resources. It then subtracts CAD 40,000 of base payments and the CAD 6,000 extra bill. The ending project balance is negative CAD 2,000 under either schedule.

The headline funding amounts ask how much extra cash would need to be present at the planning start to prevent any modeled negative balance. The reference schedule needs CAD 2,000; the earlier-payment alternative needs CAD 8,000. Adding that cash at the start shifts the entire path upward. These amounts are additional to the selected CAD 20,000, not replacements for it.

A negative balance is a funding problem, not permission to overdraw or evidence that a lender will supply the difference. If borrowing is part of the actual plan, interest, fees, credit limits and repayment cash flows need their own ledger. The charts deliberately do not turn a temporary deficit into an automatic loan or ignore the cost of servicing it.

05

Test the amount and timing of the contingency

The matrix changes the extra-cost percentage and preparation time before the deposit. The reference payment split remains fixed. Waiting three months adds three saving transfers before the deposit and shifts every construction payment by three months. The build still lasts six months after its deposit date.

That is a controlled saving-time comparison. It does not assume a contractor will hold a quote, that materials will remain the same price, or that a postponed project can begin exactly when desired. The model also excludes temporary accommodation, storage, financing costs and household expenses outside the separately entered project-saving amount.

Repeat the exercise with different timing for actual changes and separate any known costs from uncertain ones. A line item already in the base estimate should not be charged again as a contingency event. Unspent contingency is retained cash; it becomes a project expense only when the assumed extra bill is actually included in the scenario. A cash reserve and a cost forecast answer different questions.

06

Connect the calendar to the contract and household reserve

Begin with a written scope and identify the amount, trigger and due date of each payment. Confirm what taxes, permits, insurance, cleanup and other agreed costs are already included. Keep records of approved changes so that the budget can be reconciled with invoices rather than memory.

Use only resources available for the project. Counting a household emergency fund as project cash reduces the cash left for other emergencies; the model does not restore it automatically. Likewise, an anticipated rebate belongs on its expected receipt date after its eligibility and processing assumptions are checked. It cannot fund an earlier invoice simply because it may eventually reduce net cost.

Review all four views before committing: bills by date, the lowest cash point, the final reconciliation and alternative contingency assumptions. The objective is a calendar with supported resources at every payment date, plus a separately understood household buffer. A renovation’s possible resale benefit does not pay the contractor’s current bill and is outside this cash-flow comparison.
